content: A fatty streak, despite its name, is not composed of fat but rather of macrophage white blood cells. It represents the earliest stage of an atheroma, as observed during autopsy when examining the inner surface of arteries without magnification. This lesion is not detectable in living humans using current imaging technologies, including intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), which has the highest spatial resolution for visualizing artery walls in vivo. The fatty streak is the first grossly visible lesion in the progression of atherosclerosis. It appears as an irregular off-white to yellow-white discoloration near the luminal surface of the artery. These streaks are not composed of fat but are instead small accumulations of monocyte-derived macrophages located beneath the inner endothelial layer of the arteries. The primary cellular component of the fatty streak is foamy macrophages, which sometimes include additional T lymphocytes, aggregated platelets, and localized smooth muscle cells. Under a microscope, these macrophages exhibit a foamy appearance due to the presence of large collections of membrane-bound vesicles within their cytoplasm. Cholesterol within cells is primarily located in the cell membranes, and the accumulation of these membranes leads to an elevated local concentration of membrane-bound cholesterol and other lipids. When viewed en masse, the foamy macrophages typically have an off-white to yellow-white color. They were historically named fatty streaks because, from a gross (non-microscopic) perspective, they were thought to resemble streaks of fat against the otherwise red or pink muscular tissue background that forms the arterial wall.
